Entertainment.title: Music streaming: Why we're listening to so many old songs
Entertainment.text:
More music is being created than at any other time in human history. Every day, more than 100,000 songs, external are being submitted to streaming services.

And despite the deluge of AI music, external - Spotify says it has removed 75 million "spammy tracks" from its catalogue - real music still makes up most of our listening. The streaming service Deezer says AI accounts for just 0.5% of streams on its platform.

The problem for all those artists creating new music is that our listening habits increasingly show a love for nostalgia.

Luminate, an independent entertainment data and analytics company that tracks music, film, and television consumption first started tracking music streaming in 2008.

This year, it recorded that the streaming of current music (released less than 18 months ago) was significantly dwarfed by older music in both the UK and US.

In the first half of 2026, almost two thirds of the music played (about 60%) was released five or more years ago.

So, if we're stuck in a streaming rut, what's to blame?

In the UK, most of us seem to be shunning new songs.

Eighteen of the year's top 20 bestselling songs, external were released 12 months ago, or earlier.

The year's eighth biggest hit is Zara Larsson's Lush Life, which originally came out in June 2015. Michael Jackson's Billie Jean (1983) is in 22nd place. Fleetwood Mac's Dreams (1977) is 30th.

It's a sign that, with practically every song ever recorded available at the press of a button, people are increasingly seeking out the classics - or what the music industry categorises as "deep catalogue".

It's a similar story in the US.

There, in the two most-played genres, R&B and Hip-Hop, external, about 60% of streams are old-school catalogue hits.

Likewise, in America, Ella Langley's Choosin' Texas has become the longest-running number one in US chart history.

The reality, of course, is that hits need to achieve "millions of streams a day, external" to reach the top of the charts.

But according to the UK's Competition and Markets Authority, nearly two thirds of streams are of music recorded by "only the top 0.4% of artists, external".

As we increasingly cling on to our favourites, aspiring artists may be suffering.

Even after a song has gone viral, some musicians say it can be hard to promote subsequent releases and sustain a career. A platform like TikTok isn't set up to boost artists, it's there to create viral moments around a single song.

"It's easier [today] for folks to be passive fans," noted J Erving, the founder of Raye's distribution company, Human Re Sources, in a recent interview with Billboard, external.

"For you to consider yourself broken [as a mainstream artist], people need to care about you beyond the song. Where is the connectivity? Are people really dialled in in a deeper way?"

It's a problem the music industry is keen to tackle.

Oliver Schusser, the Head of Apple Music, says his streaming service is working to champion "tomorrow's artists" in its curation.

"You know, we do the Super Bowl halftime show, we need to make sure that we still have performers in 10, 20, 30 years," he tells BBC News.

"Because if you look back at the performers we had in the last four years, they all started somewhere before they got to the world's biggest stage."

Other organisations like Sofar Sounds work exclusively with grassroots musicians, putting on intimate pop-up gigs in cities across the globe.

This October, its Shoreditch Sofar Fringe festival showcased a whole host of artists like East London rapper J Casa.

Chiminyo, a London-based independent artist, believes that auto-generated playlists are also misleading people into thinking they're listening to "hand-picked" tunes from bona fide artists - as opposed to digitally mass-produced sound-alikes created to catch streams.

Scrolling through a "relaxing jazz piano playlist" with over 370,000 saves on Spotify, he spots that top featured artists that rack up hundreds of thousands of monthly listens have unverified accounts.

Little - if anything - can be found about them online, he says.

To his trained ear, Chiminyo also says the different artists' tracks sound near identical, reason enough to conclude the compositions have been synthetically mass-produced.

"Its all the same: the same piano feel, the same microphone placement, the same tape machine, has been used on every single one of these tracks."

When asked, Spotify said it had rolled out platform-wide policies, external against impersonation and is working to the improve filtering out of AI-related issues on its platform. But it acknowledges AI's use in music production sits on a spectrum with some artists choosing to use it to varying degrees.

New music may not be dying out, but it's clear it has a lot to contend with in 2026.

Entertainment.title: Sam Fender calls out ticket prices ahead of 2027 tour sale
Entertainment.text:
Sam Fender has called out the price of gig tickets ahead of his next tour, promising to lower the cost.

The 32-year-old announced his Proper Massive Stadium Tour earlier this week, which will visit Newcastle, Cardiff, London, Edinburgh, Dublin and Manchester in summer 2027.

While tickets are yet to go on sale, Fender responded to a post on social media which claimed to outline the expected ticket prices.

The Geordie musician also said standing would not be split into a front and back tier and he had "no idea how this was normalised at gigs".

Tickets are due to go on general sale at 09:30 GMT on Friday, with a pre-sale at the same time on Wednesday.

But Fender said he was "not happy" with the reported prices.

"They're getting changed," he said on Instagram.

"It got inflated well more than I'd had in mind, it should only be inflated in relation to the cost of putting the show on."

The North Shields singer also said he did not want there to be an option for fans to pay more money to be closer to the front.

"The standing will not be split as well, I had no idea about it," Fender said.

"I have no idea how this was normalised in gigs... it won't be happening on this tour."

He is not the first musician to raise concerns over ticket pricing.

Zara Larsson agreed with fans earlier this year that her tickets were too expensive.

The Swedish singer said while she did not have control over the prices, she hoped she would in the future.

Entertainment.title: Celebrity Traitors, episode eight: Series left on a knife edge after a trip to the field of screams
Entertainment.text:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode eight of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

Original Celebrity Traitor Maya Jama, latest recruit King Kenny and now even the reluctant James Acaster - hooray! - have developed a real appetite for murder this week.

And going into Friday's episode we knew that their collective cruel intention was to see that one of three faithfuls, Miranda Hart, Romesh Ranganathan or Sebastian "Bash" Croft, did not make it to breakfast.

When it became clear that the murdered Miranda had danced her last dance in the castle - leaving only 10 of the initial 21 players - the pressure began to mount and speculation was rife as to whodunnit and why?

The self-declared Miss Marple wannabe had been stitched up, of course. "Miranda is a good detective," noted James A in a flashback to the turret talk from the night before.

"I don't know who I'm becoming," responded Maya - who has taken to treachery like a duck to water - "but I feel it in my loins, and Miranda is the only one that makes sense."

Miranda, who had been in her element sleuthing away on the show, did not take the news of her untimely death at all well, throwing her murder note to the ground. "No! Absolutely not," she cried.

"Oh bottoms!

"I'm so cross with myself, I was wholly focusing on my Joanne issue," she added, with reference to her theory about Joanne McNally being a traitor. One that even Miranda herself had - unwisely - "debunked" at the roundtable.

Ending on a more positive note, the comedian, who has had health issues in recent years, reflected: "Ultimately, in my little personal story, this has been quite extraordinary that I've been able to get back and do the thing that I love professionally and do the things that I love personally.

"Like wandering around a Scottish island and being in nature and laughing and connecting. There were times that I didn't think that would be possible again".

With Miss Marple now out of the picture, James A told viewers that two of the remaining traitor hunters, James Blunt and Michael Sheen are like "Holmes and Watson".

"Luckily they're completely looking in all the wrong places," he added.

Leigh-Anne, having lost her new Big Mix dance partner from episode six, said she was now praying that the heat on her would now cool down.

While Miranda was being murdered on Thursday night, out in the real world another Little Mix star Jade Thirlwell told BBC News - at the Mercury prize ceremony - that her groupmate was a real life "faithful through and through".

Those kind words would be worth little if the now nicely positioned traitors kept going at this rate, however.

"This is actually embarrassing," declared comedian Romesh at breakfast.

"We are getting battered," a sneaky Maya agreed. "This is just getting harder and harder by the second."

Wink, wink.

Breaking character in the safety of the diary room, the Gentleman actress and presenter admitted: "I'm not gonna lie, I feel terrible about Miranda, I really do and she will be sorely missed.

"But with great honour comes great pressure, and here I am, ’OG Traits‘, still flying it up."

Joanne had earlier joked that Maya would not be killed or banished as "she's too hot. The hot ones always survive."

After breakfast, James B, who has been pretty consistently wrong with his theories throughout the series, continued his fine form, saying of Maya and Kenny: "I think they are the two most innocent."

He joked (it was a joke, right?): "Watching me in this castle must be like watching Sherlock at work."

With less heat on her than Christmas Day in Blackpool, Maya started planting a seed that roundtable "chief investigator" Michael Sheen might be up to something.

"How has that guy not been killed?" asked Romesh.

"It's like not getting rid of [Hercule] Poirot," he added, as the literary detective references kept coming.

Michael and Sharon - fast becoming a dark horse with her theory about Ross Kemp having been killed with perfume - said she was determined to catch a traitor and would "not be taking any prisoners".

On to Friday's mission, as the dwindling group arrived in a "field of screams", as presenter Claudia Winkleman aptly put it, full of scary-looking scarecrows.

"This is like the Wickerman," said Joanne. "A solo scarecrow is sinister enough. A gaggle of scarecrows is terrifying."

The task involved them attempting to retrieve bags of gold from inside the straw men with a pitchfork, in a bid to add thousands of pounds to the charity prize pot.

Joanne's knot-tying badge she claimed to have been awarded in her youth didn't seem to help her much, though, as she struggled initially to grab any gold.

"I have a newfound respect for the farming community," she declared.

But it wasn't only gold on offer, it transpired. An as-yet unrevealed game-changing power would be bestowed upon one player, but only after they had to blow up the proxy pumpkin scarecrow heads of all but three of the most trustworthy contestants.

Things got a bit awkward when poor Sharon "got so mad at the boys" - James B, Michael and Kenny - over which heads should roll.

In the most remarkably stupid moment of the series since Richard E Grant told everyone he was a traitor, the group chose to preserve the heads belonging to Maya, James A and Kenny.

"I had to hold in my laughter," said Maya, privately afterwards. "Of all people, you saved us. I just thought, 'oh my gosh, have we completed this game already? We are trusting. We are unsuspecting. We are killing you all'."

With the others en route back to the castle, Winkleman quipped to the traitors: "This is like an outdoor turret."

The special power was revealed to be a double dagger enabling "the trustworthy trio", as James A is now calling them, to award two banishment votes to whoever they wanted to hold it.

King Kenny became King Arthur being crowned keeper of the special blade.

"I think it's in the right hands," declared James B back at the castle, now colder than ever in terms of catching a traitor.

"I feel like whoever it is, they are five steps ahead of us," noted a befuddled Leigh-Anne. "We don't have a clue!"

Romesh then had to remind Joanne that her policy of not voting off Michael because he's "great company" is not really how the game should work.

With the double dagger in play and time running out for the faithful, Michael declared that he had to catch a traitor tonight.

As discussions began, double trouble Kenny warned: "Be nice to me everyone!"

"You're a powerful man," noted Joanne.

Bash, who had flown under the radar until this point, drew some heat along with Leigh-Anne and Sharon at another roundtable led my Don Michael.

"If you're a faithful, why are you still here?" Bash asked the Welshman, who noted he had a shield last time out.

Romesh agreed: "I definitely would have killed you by now if I was a traitor. And I mean that as a massive compliment, because I think, for the morale of the group, you not being here would decimate us."

In an attempt to deflect attention away from himself, Michael stressed how Sharon had been acting like a "totally different person" of late.

Kenny went along with it, sticking his double dagger into the Barbie actress. And James B voted the same way due to her "suspicious" actions earlier on.

Scotswoman Sharon received four votes, along with Irish comic Joanne, meaning that - after desperate final pleas from the pair - it went to second round.

"Do whatever youse want, it's a game," offered a seemingly defeated Sharon.

"I wish I didn't take this dagger," said Kenny, ahead of his decisive second thrust of the double blade. "But I'm gonna vote for..."

The producers then left things, quite literally, on a knife edge.

Ten contestant remain (for now): seven faithfuls (soon to be six) and three traitors, putting the cloaked interlopers in a great position going into the final two episodes.

With the hurly-burly done for another week, we will wait with baited breath until Hallowe'en's double header to see how the battle will be lost and won.

Entertainment.title: Strictly Come Dancing's new hosts: Flat-footed or fab-u-lous?
Entertainment.text:
Strictly Come Dancing's new hosting trio received a very mixed reception when the latest series began a month ago. Ratings have dipped and the jury's still out, but critics say they are slowly getting into the groove.

Changing the hosting team on the BBC's flagship Saturday night entertainment show was never likely to be a waltz in the park.

And going from two presenters to three, and giving them slightly different roles, upset the show's rhythm even more.

Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman were always going to be a hard act to follow.

Into their sparkly shoes have stepped the safe and smooth Emma Willis; the flamboyant former professional dancer Johannes Radebe; and cheeky comedian Josh Widdicombe, a wildcard who was not hitherto associated with either the dance world or prime-time TV.

Willis and Widdicombe have been paired on the live shows, where he is tasked with injecting humour into the moments before and after each dance - with mixed results, say critics.

Radebe, meanwhile, has taken over from Winkleman upstairs on the mezzanine, bringing his warmth and dance expertise to the celebrity interviews following each routine.

After they made their debuts in September, the Times' Carol Midgley billed them as, external "TV's most awkward ménage à trois".

The Daily Telegraph's Chris Bennion declared, external that Strictly's "new 'throuple' is an utter disaster", adding: "It's a mess, a muddle, a confusing pudding."

Metro's Adam Miller said, external their debut was "a triumph", however, and the i Paper's Sarah Carson wrote, external that Strictly had "played a blinder", even though the hosts "looked a little awkward as a three at times".

Widdicombe has come in for particular flack. He "felt like an awkward spare part" and looked like "the work experience boy", wrote Sasha Morris of the Daily Express, external.

And the Independent's Isobel Lewis said, external Widdicombe "is a problem the show needs to solve".

She believes things have now improved, although the show hasn't completely solved the problem.

"He's basically acting too much like a comedian to be a presenter," the freelance culture journalist tells BBC News.

"I think he's getting more comfortable with it. When it's him and Emma doing the bits when they intro each act, and they're obviously reading off an autocue, they feel way more confident there, and it feels more like it works."

The problem grows when Widdicombe does what comes naturally as a good comedian, Lewis says, and tries to be spontaneous.

"They've got, like, 20 seconds with each judge. It's such a tight amount of time, and that's what lends it to feeling sloppy and like he's constantly jumping in.

"Unfortunately it reads a bit like trying to steal attention and have the last laugh. I actually don't think that is what he's trying to do as a selfish act. I just think that is his comedic impulse."

She says it's unfair to put the criticism on Widdicombe, and says as time has gone on he feels less awkward, with comments online suggesting some fans are "warming to him".

"But at the beginning there's always that knee-jerk reaction of, 'I don't like this'," Lewis says.

Radio Times TV and podcast editor Caroline Frost agrees that the trio have gradually settled in.

"I think it's fair to say there were some bumps in the road in the first couple of episodes," she says, "but they do appear to be very slowly relaxing into their new roles."

When it comes to Willis and Widdicombe's double act, Frost would like to see more spontaneity, not less.

"They've been relying quite visibly on scripts and gags, and I would like to see them relax into themselves," she adds.

"It's completely understandable that they would be very scripted, very alert to the clock and to all of the other many demands of running a live show of that scale - but the really talented people can do that on the fly.

"Josh is very likeable, and we know he's a very funny man," she notes. "He doesn't need the shackles of the script that he's currently handcuffed to, and I would love to see him take off those cuffs and become more spontaneous."

Frost suggests sending Widdicombe upstairs to conduct the post-dance interviews instead of Radebe, who at times struggles to control his exuberant former fellow dancers. "It's a bit like when you get an internal promotion at work," she reflects.

The producers should make the most of Radebe's strengths and make him "a sort of talent pundit", she suggests.

"Have him in the rehearsal rooms, telling us what's going on. He would be a lovely middleman between what we're seeing on the dance floor and what is going on technically."

Ahead of the series, there had been reports that Radebe would be used as a "roving reporter".

Widdicombe previously suggested the trio's roles would be fluid, telling The Rest Is Entertainment it was "going to be like total football... We're going to be moving everywhere".

But while some segments are flexible - especially in the Sunday result show - their main roles appear fixed.

Some fans have been won over by Radebe since he took over Winkleman's old domain.

"JoJo has been really brilliant up in... I guess the Claudatorium, but I'm not sure what we call it now," says Flo Sayers, co-host of the Strictly on the Sofa podcast.

"He is the link to previous Strictly, and I think he has taken to that role really well. I like that he's a bit different from Claudia. He's less the comedian and more the supportive friend for the contestants when they've got off the dance floor and they're probably feeling a little bit vulnerable.

"And his fashion has been amazing, so I'm excited to see what he wears every week."

Sayers isn't sure whether the new line-up has contributed to lower ratings - about six million people are tuning in every week this year, down by about a million.

But overall, she believes that the trio are getting used to the demands of the series.

Dr Karen Wood, associate professor at the Centre for Dance Research at Coventry University, agrees and says the trio "are now really starting to feel a bit more settled".

"I think JoJo has transitioned beautifully from professional dancer to host, and obviously he comes with all his fabulousness," she says.

"He's able to talk about the technical details as well as be very supportive to the professional dancers and the celebrities. And his outfits are just marvellous. So I think he suits that role very well.

"Likewise, Emma is holding her own when she's with Josh and when she's not. She's an experienced presenter. You can you can tell.

"And Josh is bringing the humour. I know it's come with some criticism. But last week was the first week that I felt, oh, these two are actually funny."

She concludes: "It's really feeling like they're finding their stride and their rhythm with it. And I think that's going to develop more and more - very much as the celebrities do."

Just as the show's celebrity contestants improve week by week, the same may be true of the hosts - except viewers can't vote them off if they don't like them.

The next episode of Strictly Come Dancing airs on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Saturday.

Entertainment.title: Jazzy: The Irish DJ dropping her debut after a billion streams
Entertainment.text:
Releasing your first album is a big step for any artist, but for Jazzy it's one that's followed some huge strides.

The Irish singer and DJ has been streamed more than a billion times and worked with industry heavyweights including Calvin Harris.

If that's not enough, on Saturday she has her biggest gig yet when she'll be playing tracks like No Bad Vibes and Someday in front of a home crowd in Dublin.

For Jazzy, writing an album has always been in the back of her mind and now, finally, it's time to hit send.

She's previously released dozens of singles, building up a monthly listenership over 10 million strong, but Peace and Patience is her first full-length work.

"It's been quite a few years of creating some smaller projects," she tells BBC Newsbeat.

"That's given me enough experience now to feel like it was the right moment."

The 30-year-old, real name Yasmine Byrne, has been putting out music for more than five years and collabed with the likes of Sonny Fodera, Rossi. and KILIMANJARO on some of her biggest tracks.

Dance music has boomed in recent years, with Spotify previously telling Newsbeat that since 2020 the amount under-25s listen to the genre has grown by more than 73% globally.

It also dominated festival line-ups over the summer - including Radio 1's Big Weekend which dedicated all its stages to dance music on the opening night.

But artists in the genre have often moved away from albums, opting instead to release EPs and singles.

Jazzy has noticed the change, saying it feels "a lot different now, with people kind of siding with virality rather than quality of music".

"When I was making the album, I wasn't thinking about going viral or anything like that. I just wanted to make something that was true to me and sounded like a Jazzy album.

"I like to let things happen quite organically and I try to just let the music speak to me."

Jazzy is rooted in the Dublin club scene, starting her career as part of a group called Powerful Creative Minds in the city.

But as more and more clubs close, the DJ says there are fewer opportunities for artists to cut their teeth offline.

"When I first started going out, there was a lot more going on," she says.

"There was a lot more nightclubs to go to and it's very different when we look at it now, which is sad.

"There's definitely a home for dance music on the internet of course but club culture is very important and I think that's something that we need to keep going for sure."

Latest figures from the Night Time Industries Association, external suggest about 12 venues are closing across the UK every month, with almost 30% of the night time economy lost since the coronavirus pandemic.

"I hope to God that it doesn't disappear, the club scene altogether," says Jazzy, who describes a similar issue in Ireland.

"We all need to try and put a hand in to keep it going."

Jazzy's taking her new album on tour across the UK from next month, but first she has her biggest gig yet: Dublin's 3Arena in front of a home crowd.

Even after a Coachella set and supporting Calvin Harris, she describes this as the "biggest milestone of my career to date".

While she says fans can mostly expect her brand of uplifting records on the album, she says it's also more personal than her usual work.

She highlights one track in particular, Invisible, as a change from her more upbeat releases. It deals with a bad experience she had in the music industry, describing it as "like my first ever diss track".

"I hope [fans] learn a little bit more about me, because that was one of my goals with the album - to open up a little bit about experiences in life as well.

"So there's a little message from me in each song."

Entertainment.title: James Bond: Jack Lowden and Callum Turner to screen test this weekend, reports say
Entertainment.text:
Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O'Connor are among the actors thought to be taking part in final auditions to play James Bond, according to reports.

Screen tests are said to be taking place this weekend, possibly as early as Friday, according to the Hollywood Reporter, external, with between three and five actors understood to have reached the last stages of the process.

The finalists are said to be taking part in auditions with three components - stunts, camera presence and dialogue.

Deadline reported the screen tests, external had been due take place in early October, but had been delayed by scheduling conflicts, while Variety said Turner and Lowden, external "appear to be in the mix" to replace Daniel Craig.

British actors Aaron Taylor-Johnson and James Norton were previously connected to the role, while Irish actor Paul Mescal's name had also been thrown into the mix.

Other actors now appear to be in the frame, but reports on the current casting situation vary.

Variety suggested Slow Horses star Lowden may now be edging ahead, while Masters of the Air star Turner was speculated about earlier this year, with some fans suggesting his wife Dua Lipa could sing the Bond theme song.

Sources told Deadline that at least four final screen test offers have been made, and while unconfirmed, "three of the four expected to test are Jack Lowden, Callum Turner and Josh O'Connor".

O'Connor is best known for playing Prince Charles in The Crown, and for starring in 2025's Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery, with Craig.

Jack O'Connell had been thought to be in the mix, but sources said this may no longer be the case, while Euphoria and Wuthering Heights Star Jacob Elordi is not thought to be testing.

Other stars who were previously linked with the role include The King's Man star Harris Dickinson, along with SAS: Rogue Heroes' Jack Barton.

Deadline said: "Even with the tests wrapping next week, there is no timeline for when a final decision will be made."

Amazon MGM Studios, who now control the Bond franchise, announced in May, external that the casting process was under way, but had no further comment at the time.

In August, Amy Pascal, one of the next film's producers, told Deadline, external the "end of the year is a good bet" for possible news on who would be playing Bond.

"We are being really, really methodical. Having worked with Barbara Broccoli at the studio, I mean, Daniel Craig is a hard act to follow," she said.

"And it's got to be something really different that is a stirring and exciting and different."

The BBC's Lizo Mzimba reported in September that "for a series where the stakes are so high, no expense is spared in ensuring that the film team know exactly how each auditionee will come across on screen".

He added: "As the 007 team themselves have explained, external in the past: 'Bond screen tests are elaborate affairs involving hair and make-up, costumes, sets, and other actors'."

The next James Bond: The (00)7 questions fans want answered

Search for new James Bond officially kicks off as auditions begin

Only six actors have ever played novelist Ian Fleming's British Secret Service agent 007 in the official film series - Sean Connery, Roger Moore, George Lazenby, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig.

The last announcement of a new Bond was in 2005 with Craig, who last starred in the role in 2021's No Time to Die, directed by Cary Joji Fukunaga.

During the equivalent stage of the audition process two decades ago, Superman actor Henry Cavill was widely thought to have also been in the running.

"They told me I was close," Cavill told the Happy Sad Confused podcast in 2022. "They told me it was ultimately down to, and this is what I've been told, it was just down to me and Daniel, and I was the younger option.

"They obviously went with Daniel and I think it was an amazing choice to go with Daniel," he said. "I probably wasn't ready at the time and I think Daniel did an incredible job over the past movies, so I'm happy they made that choice."

The forthcoming film, reportedly out in 2028, will be directed by Dune's Denis Villeneuve, with Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight writing the script.

Knight told Zoe Ball on Greatest Hits Radio, external in September that the first draft of the script was completed.

Amazon bought MGM for $8.5bn (£6.3bn) in 2021, which included the rights to distribute James Bond, and they are reported to have paid at least $20m (£14.9m) more for the rights to creatively control Bond's future.

Pascal and David Heyman are producing the film, while Tanya Lapointe is executive producer.

Knight's final words on the film were about how much he was enjoying working on it.

He told Ball:, external "I'm absolutely loving doing it. It's an honour to be asked. And believe it's going to be so good. I really do believe it's going to be amazing."

Entertainment.title: Raye wins the Mercury Prize with This Music May Contain Hope
Entertainment.text:
Raye has won the 2026 Mercury Prize for her show-stopping second album This Music May Contain Hope.

A pop record sprinkled with golden age Hollywood glamour, it beat the likes of Sir Paul McCartney, Olivia Dean and Jade to scoop the £25,000 prize.

"I couldn't tell you how grateful I am to be holding this," said Raye, clutching her trophy at Newcastle's Utilita Arena. "I'm shaking, I'm jet-lagged, I'm tired. It's all blurry."

It is the first time a pop album has won the coveted prize - which recognises the best British or Irish album of the last 12 months - since M People's Elegant Slumming in 1994.

Speaking to the BBC afterwards, Raye said she'd "poured everything I had" into the record, which features the global hit song Where Is My Husband?

"I made this album not focusing on commercial [success], not focusing on making things cookie-cutter," said the 28-year-old.

"Some of these songs are seven minutes. They're indulgent. They're maximalist."

Across 17 tracks and 73 minutes, the record tells a cinematic story about a relationship that ends in tears on the rainy streets of Paris, then follows our plucky heroine as she dusts off the debris and emerges stronger and more resilient.

Along the way, it features both of her grandparents, the soul legend Al Green, four separate orchestras and more than 100 musicians.

But the album almost never happened. Two years ago this week, the singer's car was stolen, along with all of her songwriting notebooks and demos.

Although they were eventually recovered, it delayed work on This Music May Contain Hope by almost a year.

Looking back, she was philosophical about the delay.

"I was distraught. I was very worried, but you know, it all turned out great.

"Every little slip, every little accident, every little thing, it creates the path that you take.

"And it's easy to spend time wishing things were the other way. But right now, I certainly do not."

In the run-up to this year's ceremony, Olivia Dean had been the bookmakers' favourite for her second album, The Art of Loving.

An easy-going, soulful collection of love songs, it had already been named album of the year at the Brit Awards and the Mobos, and is widely expected to earn the singer a Grammy nomination in the same category next month.

Speaking backstage, the singer said she was overwhelmed by the success.

"I don't think I've processed it yet, to be honest," she said. "I feel like I'm still in this crazy whirlwind of it all.

"And maybe, when I take a break over Christmas, I'll reflect on the sofa."

Other nominees included the rapper Kojey Radical, Geordie jazz act Knats, and former Little Mix star Jade - who was the first ever X Factor winner to receive a Mercury nomination.

The shortlist also included the charity compilation album Help (2), recorded in aid of Warchild, which featured new music and cover versions by artists such as Olivia Rodrigo, Damon Albarn, Depeche Mode and The Last Dinner Party.

The tracklist also included nine former Mercury Prize winners: Arctic Monkeys, Young Fathers, Wolf Alice, Pulp, Sampha, Portishead's Beth Gibbons, Arlo Parks, English Teacher and Ezra Collective.

Last year, the prize was won by Newcastle singer-songwriter Sam Fender, who donated his £25,000 winnings to grassroots music venues, helping to support up-and-coming songwriters around the UK.

Entertainment.title: Prince William makes surprise appearance on Graham Norton
Entertainment.text:
The Prince of Wales has made a surprise appearance on the Graham Norton Show, as part of a special edition to mark the Earthshot Prize.

During the episode, which airs on Friday, he joined Cate Blanchett, Robert Irwin and Hannah Waddingham, who are all involved with the prize.

As Norton spoke about the initiative with the trio he surprised the audience by then inviting the prince out to join them on the sofa, to cheers and gasps from the audience.

They discussed the need to pair optimism and urgency when tackling climate change. The prize was founded by William to "celebrate and scale the solutions that will repair our planet".

The guests also chatted about William's long-time support for Aston Villa, and his love of Christopher Nolan films.

William set up the Earthshot Prize in 2020, drawing inspiration from US President John F Kennedy's Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to get astronauts to the Moon and back safely.

There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature, Clean Our Air, Revive Our Oceans, Build a Waste-Free World and Fix Our Climate. Each winner receives £1m.

The future king has committed himself to the prize until 2030. This year's winners will be announced at a ceremony in Mumbai in November.

Last year, the ceremony for the prizes drew famous faces such as former Formula 1 driver Sebastian Vettel and then-UK prime minister Keir Starmer. Pop stars Kylie Minogue and Shawn Mendes performed at the ceremony in Rio de Janeiro.

The 2025 winners included Lagos Fashion Week, for "transforming one of the world's most wasteful industries" by requiring designers to demonstrate their commitment to sustainability.

At last year's ceremony, William said the winners were "proof that progress is possible".

Entertainment.title: Great Pottery Thrown Down stars to marry in Pwllheli home after proposal 'on Welsh soil'
Entertainment.text:
The Great Pottery Throw Down judge Keith Brymer Jones has told how he and his partner are to marry in their north Wales chapel home after he proposed to her "on Welsh soil".

Jones said he and actor Marj Hogarth, who are renovating a Grade II-listed chapel in Pwllheli, were on tour "and I just thought I ought to really propose to her on Welsh soil".

He proposed during their show at the New Theatre in Cardiff, and "the idea is to get married in the main hall some time in May of next year".

The ceramicist also said there were a lot of derelict chapels across Wales and "we need to repurpose these buildings and give them a new lease of life".

Jones has previously said he felt the move to Wales was like coming back to his "roots" as his parents were from Swansea and Cardiff.

He said Wales had inspired him to get into ceramics, with his mum having had a passion for pottery too.

He told BBC Radio Wales that he remembered driving down Welsh country lanes in search of pottery when he was growing up.

Jones and Hogarth, an actor, bought 163-year-old Capel Salem on the Llŷn Peninsula in 2022 and have been transforming it into their dream home, alongside a pottery studio and community space.

Jones said he found Capel Salem while "trawling the internet" and he and Hogarth drove up to see it the following day and "fell in love with the place".

He said the Grade II-listed 8,500sq ft building was their "forever home" and in "quite a magical place" on the north Wales coast, with Pwllheli overlooking Eryri and Yr Wyddfa.

"We've been living there for about a year and a half and we absolutely love it," he said, adding that the community in Pwllheli had been "absolutely amazing".

Entertainment.title: Tom Skerritt, star of Top Gun and Alien, dies aged 93
Entertainment.text:
US actor Tom Skerritt, who starred in the TV series Picket Fences and the films Alien and Top Gun, has died aged 93, his family says.

Skerritt died on Wednesday of natural causes, his family said, adding: "While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humour, curiosity, wisdom, generosity and the love he brought into our lives."

In a six-decade career, he appeared in the film Mash, A River Runs Through It and Ted. He also co-founded TheFilmSchool in Seattle to support next-generation filmmakers and storytellers.

His family said he will be remembered "for his belief that stories can help people heal, find purpose and create change".

The moustachioed star of several 20th Century hit films was born in 1933 in Detroit, Michigan, and served in the US Air Force before pursuing an acting career that boasted several military roles.

He made his film debut in 1962 alongside a young Robert Redford ​in War Hunt and years later reunited with Redford in the 1992 period drama A River Runs Through It, which starred Brad Pitt.

Skerritt's breakthrough role came when he played US army surgeon Duke Forrest in the 1970 Korean War comedy Mash, which also starred Donald Sutherland, Elliott Gould and Sally Kellerman.

The hit film, which was released amid unrest over the Vietnam War, was nominated for five Academy Awards and was adapted for television two years later.

He also starred alongside Sigourney Weaver in the 1979 sci-fi film Alien, which earned two Oscar nominations, and led to three sequels and several crossover projects.

"It is spontaneity and impulse ​that make the difference, and that is ⁠what I felt we had with 'Alien'," Skerritt said in a 2019 interview, according to news agency Reuters.

"Every one of us had that immediate rapport with each other."

Skerritt said that one of the things he liked most when he first read the script was that "the woman becomes a hero", referring to Weaver's character, Ripley.

During his career, he starred opposite several strong female leads.

He appeared with Shirley MacLaine in the 1977 film Turning Point and played Sally Field's husband in 1989's Steel Magnolias.

As Cdr Mike "Viper" Metcalf in the 1986 classic Top Gun, the versatile actor appeared alongside a young Tom Cruise.

On television, he won an Emmy Award in 1993 for his role as Sheriff Jimmy Brock in David E Kelley's drama Picket Fences.

The quirky procedural's ensemble cast was nominated for Sag Awards in 1995 and 1996 and he received a nod for male actor in a drama series in 1995.

Lauren Holly, who played Skerritt's deputy on Picket Fences, described him in a tribute as "our leader".

"His example made those years such a joy and we all loved and respected him so much," Holly wrote.

"He cared deeply for his family - both the one at home and the one at work. He cared deeply for his planet and all of its inhabitants. He had a huge impact on my life and so many memories I have of him include sharing fits of crippling laughter."

Skerritt also had guest roles on the small screen in The West Wing, Madam Secretary, Law & Order: SVU and Huff. He reteamed with Field as the family patriarch, William Walker, in the drama Brothers & Sisters from 2007-09.

Entertainment.title: Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit
Entertainment.text:
A US judge has ordered Donald Trump to answer questions under oath in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by 11 December.

The US president is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021.

Trump cancelled a previous deposition - an interview under oath - on 16 October, citing "matters of national importance".

But a lawyer representing the BBC said in court that Trump was campaigning in Georgia that day and had "prioritised that" over answering their questions.

Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is in the phase known as "discovery", in which the two sides provide internal or other records that could form evidence.

Charles Tobin, a lawyer for the BBC, told a court in Miami on Thursday that with two months left in the discovery period, Trump had still not completed a deposition.

US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett said Trump must sit for the deposition by 11 December or face sanctions - the most extreme of which could be the dismissal of the lawsuit - unless the discovery period is extended.

In US law, a deposition is an out-of-court statement made under oath in response to questions, which is recorded for use in later proceedings. Depositions carry legal weight - they are recorded verbatim by a court reporter and the transcripts can later be used as evidence in trials.

They typically take place in a lawyer's office without a judge physically present.

In defamation cases, lawyers for both sides are normally present for depositions.

Last week, lawyers asked that Lett compel Trump to face deposition after the last scheduled meeting did not take place.

On that day, Trump attended a midterms campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia and a fundraiser at his Mar-a-Lago property in Florida.

In a separate filing on Wednesday, Trump's lawyers said that the president could appear for the interview between 11 and 22 January next year and claimed the BBC was "wrong to claim that President Trump is avoiding his deposition in this action".

Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.

The BBC apologised for the error and said that the broadcast gave "the mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action".

The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US.

In July, Trump's lawyers conceded they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service - as they originally claimed - or on the BBC's website, BBC Select or through US broadcasters.

Trump ultimately agreed to drop the lawsuit against BBC Studios, the broadcaster's commercial arm, after the BBC argued that it had "no role in creating or producing the documentary".

Entertainment.title: ‘It annoys people when I eat’: Siobhán McSweeney on perfect snacks, parental pressure – and the power of being ‘a delicious fatty’
Entertainment.text:
Siobhán McSweeney is teaching me her preferred way to enjoy a packet of cheese and onion crisps. She has arranged two matching slabs of Cadbury’s Dairy Milk chocolate, two piles of Tayto crisps and two cans of Guinness on the table in front of us – and is issuing strict instructions. “Don’t swallow!” she booms theatrically, and I freeze, my mouth full of Taytos. The trick, McSweeney explains, is to get the crisps, chocolate and Guinness into your mouth at the same time, and then swill it all around a bit to make a kind of boozy, oniony soup. “See?” McSweeney is watching me carefully to check I am putting all the ingredients into my mouth in the correct order. “It’s delicious! Just delicious!”

McSweeney burst into the public consciousness back in 2018 with Derry Girls, a comedy series about a group of Catholic schoolgirls, set against the background of the Troubles in 1990s Northern Ireland. McSweeney won a Bafta playing the girls’ headmistress, Sister Michael – a potty-mouthed, judo-loving nun – and can count Martin Scorsese as a fan. Asked for a TV recommendation during a panel discussion in 2022, the director name-checked Derry Girls and then lifted his fist in the air in a kind of salute, exclaiming rapturously, “Those nuns!”

I have spent so many hours watching McSweeney in character as Sister Michael that it is almost a shock to see her without a nun’s habit. We are meeting today, in a conference room in London, because McSweeney is taking over from Grace Dent as the new host of the Guardian’s food podcast, Comfort Eating. I arrived at the interview with a multipack of Taytos, a family‑size Dairy Milk and two cans of Guinness in my bike bag, because McSweeney chose this concoction as her favourite snack when she appeared on the podcast as a guest, back in 2021. She also told a story about eating a caterpillar that had fallen from her moth-infested ceiling into her stir‑fry, purely because she couldn’t be bothered to fish it out. “Listen: protein,” she says today, remembering that caterpillar. “Free protein where you can.”

Since Derry Girls, the actor has made a habit of portraying slightly intimidating women. She plays the achingly sarcastic celebrity chef Della Fry in Amandaland, and hosts the Irish version of The Traitors, in which she commands a pack of wolfhounds and wears a lot of ruffs. But today, McSweeney’s short, silver‑grey hair is brushed back from her face and she is dressed casually, in trousers and a simple top. Sister Michael is always lolling back in her chair and surveying you sardonically across a desk – but the real McSweeney leans forward and asks a lot of questions.

It is lunchtime, so I have brought a takeaway from the Indian restaurant Dishoom with me, as well as the Taytos. “I love doing this podcast because it annoys people when I eat,” McSweeney says, tucking into a fish curry. Part of the reason why she accepted the job as host of Comfort Eating, she explains, is because visibly enjoying her food – as a woman who is not stick-thin – is a kind of provocation. “They’ve been told that somebody like me should not feel good about themselves,” she says, grinning toothily at me. “Being a delicious fatty.”

Ever since she first arrived at drama school, in the early 2000s, people have been telling McSweeney to lose weight. “Agents, casting directors, teachers” – McSweeney checks the list off for me now, almost breezily. “I have been different sizes but it’s never been an acceptable size,” she says. “‘Unruly’ I call it – there’s sort of an unruliness that has been forced upon my body that I don’t feel about it, but other people feel it’s unruly and it doesn’t behave.” All the other girls at her drama college were starving themselves, McSweeney remembers now. “They were starving in secondary school as well – it was the 90s! I don’t know how I managed to escape it.” She is grinning at me again. “I don’t think I have the willpower to not eat. I don’t really have much discipline.”

It strikes me that continuing to like yourself and your body, in the face of such vicious scrutiny, is not so much a failure of will as its opposite – proof that McSweeney has a will of absolute iron. Responding to a particularly poisonous bout of online criticism of her looks back in 2023, McSweeney delivered a kind of masterclass in the art of self-worth, tweeting: “I’m really lovely. I like my hair. And I like food. And I’m not sorry I’m loud. I thought feminism fights for me to be loud. And my accent is gorgeous. My teeth are yellow and wonky that’s true. But I sorta don’t care. And sure are you perfect?”

McSweeney says she wouldn’t even bother to respond to online abuse like that these days, because “it’s so insane now on social media. There is no honesty to it because we don’t know if they are bots or not.” But when I push her on the willpower point, and suggest that there is something inherently political about refusing to lose weight in her industry, she agrees with me. “I do get perverse pleasure in [responding to those] people who expect me to feel bad – by insulting me, by calling me ‘fat’ – by going, ‘And?’”

McSweeney also credits her mother, who she describes as “the kind of mam who would be round the back having a cigarette reading Dostoevsky”, with teaching her to aspire to a version of womanhood that wasn’t about appealing to men. “She wasn’t interested in me having boyfriends that much – she was, like, men will come, men will go; it’s fine.”

“She just instilled this utter independence in me that didn’t centre in any way on a romantic relationship.” McSweeney pauses for a moment here, and seems to reconsider. “I mean … she wasn’t completely immune to all that. No one is strong enough to combat that, you know? And there would be a bit of, ‘Would you not brush your hair?” McSweeney is putting on her mother’s voice now and making pleading motions. “Please, just briefly! Just give it a quick brush!”

Siobhán McSweeney grew up in County Cork, Ireland. Her father was a civil servant and her mother ran a cottage industry baking bread and cakes to sell to local shops, so the young Siobhán woke up every day to the smell of fresh soda bread. But, like any teenager worth their salt, McSweeney only wanted what she couldn’t have. “I went to the neighbours at one point because they had white sliced pan and red jam, and I thought, they’re so lucky, I have to go home now and have my freshly baked brown soda bread and my local butter,” she says. Her mother would make her school lunch every day with bread so fresh it was still warm. McSweeney remembers looking at her lunchbox and thinking “no one suffers more than me”.

McSweeney knew from an early age that she wanted to act. She says that as a child she would wish on a star every night that she would become an actor, and tells me that she once spent an entire day at school pretending she was in a sitcom, pausing every now and again to play the laugh track in her head. “Or I’d look to the camera” – she mimes whirling her head around to lock eyes with an imaginary film crew. “How obnoxious! What a pest to be around.”

McSweeney’s parents, however, had other plans for her. “We didn’t know anyone who was an actor. People on the telly didn’t look like me, didn’t sound like me,” she says. “My parents were, like, so what would that mean? You would do the panto once a year? You’re meant to work!”

Speaking to the Irish Times in August, McSweeney said that anybody in the creative industries has “an angel and a devil on your shoulder, and the devil quite often is your parents going, ‘Don’t embarrass us.’” Did she feel as if her parents were embarrassed about her? “Yeah, absolutely yeah – it’s embarrassing to have your child standing up there making a tit of themselves,” she says. “Also, Ireland in the 80s, you blend in – the idea of standing out is quite … ” she tails off thoughtfully. “I think it was a protective idea – when you are in the open you are open to abuse and people taking advantage. All these things are true and I understand fully why any parent wouldn’t want that for their child.”

McSweeney was virtually unknown before the release of Derry Girls, which came out after her 40th birthday. She tells me that in a strange way she is pleased that fame came later in life for her, because she knows people “who have achieved success very early on in their career and their heads are turned”. But the years she spent trying and failing to get parts were gruelling. “I taught, I waitressed, I pulled pints, I went on the dole, I worked at music festivals,” she says. “And I was shit at every single one of them.”

She remembers being particularly “shit” at the waitressing. “Sure, I didn’t know anything about food. I was pouring the wine the way my parents would drink wine, which would be wine right up to the top of the glass, and I didn’t know about al dente,” she says. “I thought, who is this Al Dente?”

There was a point in the 2010s when she considered giving up acting completely. “I hadn’t worked in over a year and I had just got a litany of nos,” she remembers. “And now it’s getting harder and harder for not-rich people to be an actor.” McSweeney had received grants from the EU and a scholarship to study drama at the Central School of Speech and Drama – and that kind of funding literally doesn’t exist any more. “I get really panicky thinking about the other Siobháns who don’t get what they’re meant to do,” she says, and her face is unusually serious for a moment – but then she looks at me and her eyes begin to twinkle. “I mean it should be better, it should be a bit more useful than being a clown – but, you know, it’s what I’m meant to do.”

Part of the struggle when she was being rejected at auditions was the lack of decent roles available for women. In previous interviews, McSweeney has said that casting directors explicitly told her that even though she was the funniest person in the audition room, they were going to give the part to a “prettier, younger, less funny” woman. “I graduated into a world where I really hoped somebody had a girlfriend because there was no way on earth a programme was going to centre on a woman,” she says to me now. But she wouldn’t even be in the running for the girlfriend part because “they wanted somebody who was more ‘girlfriend material’, ie, more acceptable – so, bland and pretty”.

McSweeney says she would never be considered for the main character, “always the satellite”. She rolls her eyes. “And now I’m the mother.”

McSweeney tells me that she is deliberately taking on more presenting work because properly meaty, complex acting roles for women on TV are still so rare. As well as The Traitors Ireland, McSweeney hosts The Great Pottery Throw Down. She landed the job after an appearance on a Great British Bake Off festive special in which she had a meltdown over making a trifle and ended up sitting on a bench with Sandi Toksvig, drinking champagne (“They went, that’s who we want”).

McSweeney is also an acclaimed theatre actor. She played opposite her Derry Girls co-star Nicola Coughlan last year in The Playboy of the Western World at the National Theatre, and says that being onstage is what she has always enjoyed the most (she remembers being a child and “seeing red curtains on the telly and having a funny feeling in my belly”). But presenting is “work I find interesting – and it also pays more than the theatre”, she says, with characteristic honesty.

Presenting jobs pay better than TV shows do, too – even the most successful ones. McSweeney has said publicly “I think I got 40 quid” in residuals when Derry Girls sold to Netflix. The programme has been viewed for a total of 17.3m hours on the platform. Can that figure possibly be true? McSweeney nods enthusiastically. “When Netflix bought it we got fuck all!”

When she was 27, McSweeney lost her mother, who never saw her daughter succeed as an actor. In her Bafta acceptance speech, which has been viewed 467,000 times on YouTube, McSweeney told a story about how, as her mother lay dying, she pleaded with her to retrain as a teacher. “If she could see me now, winning a Bafta for playing a teacher,” she said, wearing a red vinyl dress and laughing, lifting her bare arm above her head to punch the air with her award: “Joke’s on you, Mam!”

Would her mother feel pride, if she could see her daughter now? Or relief? “Er, relief,” says McSweeney, quick as a flash. Then she pauses for a second. “And I think she would like … I have a lot of opinions and she would like the way I speak about certain opinions.” In the same Bafta speech, McSweeney thanked the people of Derry, calling out the “ignorance and stupidity” of their political leadership, and she is a vocal critic of both English and Irish policy. Last year she was among those who campaigned successfully for the thousands of UK-based survivors of the work camps for “fallen women” that were in operation until the 90s in Ireland – known as the Magdalene laundries – to be given compensation without losing their rights to benefits.

Would her mother have been proud of her feminism? “I think she would have been as close to proud as I would allow her to be,” says McSweeney, almost shyly. “And my dad, too … He was a natural feminist rather than a learned one – couldn’t think of anything I couldn’t do because of my gender, that would make no sense to him.”

Her father died in 2018. McSweeney moved back into the family home to live with him during his final illness. She drew on those experiences to make Spud in 2024, a beautiful, surprisingly funny short film about a middle-aged woman caring for her dying father (McSweeney summarises the plot, with fabulous bluntness, as being about “an unfuckable woman who is rural and who cleans her daddy in a bath”).

In one particularly tender scene, the father and the daughter, who is played by McSweeney herself, sit eating rice pudding together in front of the telly. Was that drawn from life? Was food a comfort for them both during that time? “The really sad thing about illness is that it often takes your appetite away,” she says. “I found it with my mum, too: her appetite went towards the end.” She tells me a story about sneaking a carbonara into the hospital to give to her mother, and the sadness of her not being able to eat it. “She was so beautiful and everybody’s mam is beautiful, but she ended up with a flat belly – and I was, like, what use is a flat belly? I want a lovely big belly.”

Right at the end of Spud, McSweeney’s character finds out her father has died, and the camera closes in on her face. There is pain there but there is also something else: she is smiling slightly. It’s a great moment because it is so unexpected – and so honest. You can see in the daughter’s expression that, on some level, her father’s death has come as a relief. “I remember when my dad died, I was sort of manic for about six months because I suddenly was free, and I was grieving, but I was also free,” McSweeney says. In the immediate aftermath of her father’s death, McSweeney was bursting with ideas for new projects. “With no parents, you don’t feel like you’re letting the entire family down if you say or do something.”

Between 2018 and 2021, McSweeney went through a period that she has described – in a moment of understatement worthy of Sister Michael herself – as containing lots of “life stuff”. Her aunt, who had been a kind of surrogate mother to her, died the year after she lost her father. In 2019, her London flat burned down because of a faulty plug adaptor. Then, in 2021, in the middle of filming a Kathy Burke-directed crime drama, Holding, she broke her leg so badly that at one point the doctors thought they would have to amputate it.

How did she cope? “We place romantic and biological relationships at the heart of our sort of experience,” says McSweeney, but it was her friends who got her through it. She tells me that when she was struggling the most, she became furious with one of her friends and accused him of talking about her behind her back with the rest of the group. “I was, like, ‘Are you all talking about me?’” She puts her hands on her hips here and mimes outrage, and then she switches characters so she can play her friend’s role: “And he was, like, ‘Yeah! We’re meant to do that! We care about you! We’re making sure you’re OK, we’re asking each other, how do you think she’s doing?’”

McSweeney talks about this being a moment of realisation. She saw that friendship has an elasticity and a resilience that no romantic relationship can ever really have. “You have a fight with your boyfriend and that could destroy the relationship, right?” she says. “You have a fight with your friend, you go into your respective corners, you sulk. You call other friends. You bitch about each other. Then you go back, you have a coffee, you get drunk!”

McSweeney’s friends are annoyed with her at the moment, because she is getting her kitchen redone in her new flat, and she is refusing to install a dishwasher – as a way of preventing them from popping in for meals. “I don’t want you coming over and eating my food,” she says. She has described herself as a “sociable misanthrope” in previous interviews. As much as she loves her friends, she is not that fond of cooking and cleaning for them. I tell her I like going to other people’s homes and letting them cook for me, and then leaving without doing any washing up at all. “I bet you do!” she says. “It’s horrible for the other person – get out of my house!”

So who does she cook for? “Myself!” she says, looking me right in the eye – and for the first time there is a kind of challenge in her voice. She doesn’t like to talk about any romantic partners.

She lives alone in a flat she recently bought in London. What does she cook for herself? “It’s so boring, but I’ve been working so hard for the last five years that all my food is comfort food and I try to make it as healthy as possible,” she says. She makes a lot of bone broth and a lot of ramen. “Also, I like white bread toasted till it’s nearly black, with Kerrygold butter” – but the butter has to be sliced extremely thickly, she specifies. It has to be “sliced like cheese”.

We’re nearly out of time – and Dair y Milk. McSweeney has been hospitably breaking off slabs of chocolate and handing them to me every few minutes for the last half hour, so I can keep making Guinness-crisp soup in my mouth. I’ve got time for just one final question, so I ask McSweeney what she is looking forward to. “I’ve got my first day off for 26 days tomorrow,” she says, “but I’ve got nothing in the fridge.” She plans to go to a bakery round the corner and buy some freshly made soda bread. Ironically, after all that teenage rebellion, she likes it now. Would her mother be pleased to look down on her doing that? “Yes,” she says. “And I’m going to buy it with the money I earned being a clown.”

She has arranged two matching slabs of Cadbury’s Dairy Milk chocolate, two piles of Tayto crisps and two cans of Guinness on the table in front of us – and is issuing strict instructions. “Don’t swallow!” she booms...

BreakingNewsTab.title: UK weather: Amber warnings kick in as Storm Boelo to bring 80mph wind gusts
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Amber weather warnings have come into force in Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England as Storm Boelo continues to move across the UK, with wind gusts up to 80mph forecast in the worst-hit areas.

Strong winds and heavy showers will intensify through Saturday night, with widespread gusts expected.

The amber warning for Scotland and England will stay in place until 21:00 on Sunday, bringing an increased risk of travel disruption and potential risk to life.

The second named storm in as many days comes as National Grid continues to restore power to thousands of properties in south-west England after the area was hit hardest by Storm Austen.

The National Grid said on Saturday that more than 124,000 properties had been restored with power supplies since the beginning of the storm. However, hundreds were still without power on Saturday evening.

In north-west England, more than 2,000 properties were without power on Saturday night due to the storm.

Strong winds could cause power cuts, flying debris, damage to buildings and trees, travel disruption and danger to life from large waves, the Met Office said.

The strongest winds affected western Scotland first, and are expected to spread eastwards overnight and through Sunday.

By Saturday evening, wind gusts of 75mph had been reached at South Uist Range, Western Isles, Highland and Eilean Siar, Scotland, on Saturday, according to the Met Office.

Train and ferry services have been cancelled in Scotland and police have warned against unnecessary road journeys. Dozens of flood warnings and alerts were in place across the country and flooding also closed a number of roads, including the A78 Inverkip Road in Greenock; the A77 at Lendalfoot in Ayrshire; and several in Dumfries and Galloway.

The Met Office has warned that being outside in high winds could make people "more vulnerable to injury", stating: "Stay indoors as much as possible. If you do go out, try not to walk, or shelter, close to buildings and trees."

Parts of Northern Ireland have also been issued with an amber warning until 10:00 on Sunday.

Meanwhile, yellow rain warnings have been issued for the south-west, north-west and south-east of England, the West Midlands and Wales until 23:00 on Saturday.

Much of the north of England and Scotland has a yellow wind warning in place, which is set to last until 21:00 on Sunday, and Northern Ireland's yellow wind warning will be in place until midday on Sunday.

It has emerged that an oil tanker sailing 350 nautical miles off the Isle of Mull with 21 people on board issued a distress alert to the HM Coastguard because of "large swells" on Saturday afternoon.

"A Royal Air Force (RAF) aircraft was sent to investigate and established communications with the vessel," a spokesperson for the UK's Coastal & Maritime Agency said in a statement, without detailing from which country the ship was flagged.

The statement continued: "It was determined that there was no need for assistance, and that the vessel would continue with onwards passage."

Events across the country planned for this weekend have been cancelled due to the weather, and a number of travel disruptions have been reported.

In Merseyside, a River of Light event has been called off for the second day in a row, and Knowsley Safari Park has announced that it will close on Sunday due to "high winds".

Several markets across the North West have also been cancelled due to the weather, including Quayside Makers Market in Salford and Macclesfield Treacle Market in Cheshire.

Dublin Airport in Ireland has cancelled several outbound and inbound flights and ferry providers such as StenaLine, Irish Ferries and P&O Ferries have cancelled a number of ferry crossings in the Irish Sea.

Jason Kelly, the Met Office's chief forecaster, said: "People should prepare for the potential for disruption, particularly to travel and power supplies. Secure loose items outside, plan ahead if you are travelling and keep up to date with the latest forecast and warnings for your area."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Meghan broke contact with father in letter citing abuse claims
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The Duchess of Sussex broke contact with her father last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls, the BBC understands.

Sources close to the duchess said Meghan warned Thomas Markle in a letter that he would never meet his grandchildren.

It is understood the letter was sent to Markle, 82, while he was in hospital in the Philippines after having his leg amputated.

It has been reported that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Markle had been found in his former home in the Philippines and UK police in 2019 told Meghan about claims of abuse against him. Markle, who is based in the US, denies all such allegations.

Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018. He pulled out of his daughter's royal wedding that year, citing ill health.

The letter sent in 2025 appears to be the end of what has been a troubled relationship between father and daughter.

It is understood details of the letter, first reported in the Sun on Sunday, external, include Meghan telling Markle that he would never meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lillibet, with Meghan making it clear she would never contact her father again.

She also apparently told her father that authorities were aware of the claims made against him.

Philippines officials have confirmed they are investigating the allegations about Meghan's father, telling the BBC on Friday that its anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force was investigating the matter.

Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately said national police had secured Thomas Markle's computer and would carry out a digital forensic examination.

Meanwhile, Thomas Markle has given an interview to the Mail on Sunday, external in which he acknowledged paying for sex in the Philippines but denies sleeping with underage girls and ever possessing child abuse images.

It comes as the Metropolitan Police confirmed on Saturday it received a letter making a "number of claims" relating to Meghan's father in 2019.

The force said it shared the letter with the Duke and Duchess of Sussex at the time, although it did not pass on the contents to other law enforcement agencies.

The Met said it is now reviewing its handling of the matter.

In a statement shared on Friday, Markle revealed the existence of the letter – saying it contained "disturbing allegations" about her father.

"I am deeply distressed," Meghan wrote. "My thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."

She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

Meghan is the only daughter of Thomas Markle and her mother Doria Ragland.

Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes.

He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having his leg amputated.

The Sun reported Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jnr claimed he found a stash of images belonging to his father at his former Philippines home.

He is said to have told police he discovered child abuse videos and pictures among the items. He is understood to have contacted the US Federal Bureau of Investigations (FBI) about it in July.

The FBI has since confirmed it is aware of the allegations.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The prime minister says he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and European Union.

Speaking to the Sunday Times, Andy Burnham said he wants pursue a new type of relationship with Brussels, potentially including full EU membership or joining the single market, which would require free movement.

"I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this," he told the newspaper.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said there could be "no return" to free movement after the 2016 EU referendum, while Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the prime minister's comments were a betrayal of voters who supported Brexit.

Burnham has previously committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

He has said that any fundamental changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.

Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the "leave" campaign raising issues about rules allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.

But the prime minister suggested the type of migration experienced during the years of EU membership was "different" from the challenges faced now.

"It was generally younger people, not always, but spending a few years, then going back," he said in his told the Sunday Times., external

"And obviously the ease of that worked for British people as well."

He acknowledged that freedom of movement "had very significant challenges associated with it".

"Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different," he said.

"The balance of migration has changed, hasn't it, since then? I think we've just got to have an honest discussion about those things."

Burnham's willingness to re-open some of the most sensitive debates in British politics has been a feature of his first months in power.

In an interview with the BBC in September, Burnham said Britain could go "all the way" towards rejoining the European Union.

However, in his latest remarks, the prime minister stressed: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."

The Schengen Agreement allows passport-free travel across EU countries. While the UK did not previously abandon the pound while it was an EU member, the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the single currency.

The remarks were made ahead of his meeting with EU chiefs at a summit on 20 November in Brussels, where he is expected to pitch options for a reset of relations with the bloc.

The shadow home secretary said EU free movement would amount to "handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe".

Philp said: "The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it."

Burnham won the Greater Manchester seat of Makerfield at a by-election in June, ahead of him becoming prime minister the following month. The constituency voted to leave the European Union in 2016.

As a candidate in the by-election, Burnham had promised not to "re-run" Brexit arguments and said he was "not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU".

In response to the Sunday Times interview, Farage said: "This is a total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch".

"He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty," the Reform UK leader added.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Almost 1,000 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Nearly 1,000 arrests were made as hundreds of thousands of people took part in another day of protests across France which were followed by some clashes late on Saturday, officials have said.

After a day of largely peaceful demonstrations, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in a number of cities including Paris, while barricades were set alight in Marseille and people ripped boards from a shop in Bordeaux.

But officials have so far managed to avoid rioting and looting on the scale seen last weekend, which resulted in some of the worst scenes of disorder in France's modern history.

The interior ministry said an estimated 410,000 people protested on Saturday, while the unions put the number at about 800,000.

Some 70,000 police officers were deployed and restrictions imposed in several cities to prevent the latest protests over the cost of living and poor school conditions from descending into the kind of chaos which saw officers outnumbered, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched.

President Emmanuel Macron had decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted. Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings in recent days.

Clashes between protesters and riot police in Paris erupted at the end of a peaceful march from the city's Porte d'Italie towards Porte de Vincennes on Saturday, where the police operation included an elite unit that usually deals with organised crime and counter-terrorism.

Some protesters were seen erecting makeshift barricades and pelting officers with projectiles, while police baton-charged groups of masked youths who were smashing the windows of a car dealership.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that "several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters", the AFP news agency reported.

In the southern port of Marseille, rubbish bins were set ablaze and metal sheets used to block streets. A law enforcement vehicle was seen driving through a burning barricade in France's second-largest city.

Meanwhile, some protesters in dark clothing and face coverings were seen taking boards off a building to build a street barricade in the southern city of Bordeaux.

In Lyon, police used tear gas grenades to disperse a crowd which had reportedly gathered in an area deemed off-limits by the local prefecture.

"There were around 150 of us, mostly secondary school and university students. Then the tear gas came almost immediately. You could barely see anything in the street," said one protester in France's third-largest city.

Nuñez said late in the day that nearly 1,000 people had been arrested, a number he said would increase.

The minister also said two people had been "seriously injured": one in the south-western city of Toulouse, and another one in Clermont-Ferrand, central France.

Earlier, a peaceful protester in Paris who gave her name as Zelie told the BBC people had taken to the streets because they were "really frustrated" and had been "suffering a lot" since Macron came to office.

"They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can't say anything. Today we are in the streets because it's been too long, it's been too much," the 26-year-old said.

Two masked teenage protesters, who did not want to give their names, also said their generation was in despair and felt abandoned by the government.

"I think looting is really not good," one of the demonstrators said of last Saturday's disorder. "But it's because of poverty and the violence of the police."

He added that the protests would end "when we have a response to our demands. We really want a change in France".

Around 550,000 people took part in last weekend's demonstrations against rising fuel prices and the cost of living, with frustrations escalating after weeks of student protests. The chaos which followed resulted in more than 2,500 arrests.

Marches were initially largely peaceful but became marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction, with more than 2,000 shops and other businesses across France said to have been directly impacted. The damage was estimated "at hundreds of millions euros", France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.

One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency, while about 1,000 police officers were injured.

The French authorities later said they were forced to impose overnight curfews in Paris and other cities.

The continuing protests come ahead of France's presidential elections in six months' time, and leading contenders have levelled the blame at Macron and his ministers.
